stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: A team led by civil engineer Rosa Iglesias tested whether recycled plastic fibers could replace some of the steel mesh used to reinforce concrete sidewalks. The test slabs that contained the highest proportion of fibers and had cured for the full twenty-eight ______ fewer surface cracks after a winter of freeze-thaw cycles than did the slabs reinforced with steel mesh alone.
explanation: The subject is long: "The test slabs that contained the highest proportion of fibers and had cured for the full twenty-eight days." Its main verb is "developed." The "that" clause is essential because it tells you which slabs the sentence means, so no comma sets it off. The "and" inside that clause joins two verbs that share one subject ("contained ... and had cured"), so that doesn't call for punctuation either. Nothing should come between a subject and its verb, so the version with no punctuation is correct.

B.why: The subject is long, so you put a comma where you would pause to breathe. A comma can't separate a subject from its verb, however long the subject is. Cross out the "that" clause and you get "The test slabs, developed fewer surface cracks," which is clearly wrong.

C.why: You treated the text before the blank as a setup for what follows. A colon has to come after a complete sentence, though, and "The test slabs that contained ... twenty-eight days" is only a subject with no main verb. The colon would cut the subject off from its verb.

D.why: You used a semicolon as if two complete sentences meet at the blank. Neither side can stand alone: the left side is a subject without a main verb, and the right side is a verb phrase without a subject. A semicolon between two fragments is never correct.

subtype_name: Nothing goes here: subject–verb, verb–object, paired coordinates, essential clauses
